title: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 18 Sep 2026]
    Title:EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Frontier language models now produce professional deliverables that expert graders judge to match human work on a substantial share of economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show a measurable business effect and a large fraction of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. We argue that this is substantially a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?", whereas a deployment decision requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling - here, on our data, under our controls?". We present EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system that closes this gap. It comprises (i) a formal specification of the use case and of the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and human oversight, with an autonomy level and consequence tier that jointly set the required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that scales blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate, stated as an executable algorithm, that maps metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; and (v) a value-and-risk model in which the reviewer catch rate is a measured parameter. We report a pilot across three workflows in a global bank. In credit-memo drafting, human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort fell from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. We separate established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments required for full validation

report.summary: A new arXiv paper proposes EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system to measure whether enterprise generative AI workflows are reliable, safe, and worth scaling.
report.background: Enterprise generative AI spending has surged, but many deployments still fail to show measurable business value, and a large share of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. The paper argues this is largely a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer whether a model can perform a task, while deployment decisions require evidence that a specific workflow is fit, reliable, safe, and worth scaling on an organization's own data and controls. EnterpriseVal addresses that gap by formalizing the use case and the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, spanning model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails, and human oversight. It also introduces autonomy and consequence tiers that jointly determine how intensive evaluation must be, aiming to connect technical performance with business value and risk.
key_points: EnterpriseVal defines each use case together with a frozen socio-technical configuration: model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails, and human oversight. Autonomy level and consequence tier set the required evaluation intensity. This makes evaluation reproducible and tied to the exact deployment context rather than to general model capability.

The system includes a metric catalogue covering fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance, and oversight. It combines blinded expert grading with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference, aiming to scale expert judgment while preserving statistical rigor and reducing evaluation cost.

A two-tier threshold gate is expressed as an executable algorithm that maps metric vectors and confidence bounds to REJECT, CONDITIONAL, or SCALE decisions. A value-and-risk model treats the reviewer catch rate as a measured parameter, connecting evaluation outcomes to operational risk and business value.

In a pilot across three workflows at a global bank, credit-memo drafting reached 88% human-graded citation precision and a 1.6% hallucination rate for the best model, against gates of 70% and 5%. Procedure transformation cut estimated analyst refinement from 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. The paper separates established results, pilot evidence, proposed system elements, and open hypotheses.
report.impact: EnterpriseVal pushes the AI industry from capability benchmarking toward deployment assurance. For vendors, claims about model quality will matter less than evidence that a workflow passes context-specific reliability, safety, and value gates. For developers, it means building evaluation, logging, human-review, and confidence-interval tooling into AI products from the start, not treating evaluation as a final test. For regular users, enterprise AI may become more reliable and auditable, but also more likely to be rejected or conditionally deployed when evidence is weak. The framework could help reduce costly failed agentic projects by forcing clearer go/no-go decisions before scaling.
report.tools: Readers can explore open-source evaluation and observability tools such as Ragas, DeepEval, Promptfoo, TruLens, MLflow LLM Evaluate, LangSmith, and OpenAI Evals. For benchmark-style testing, lm-evaluation-harness and HELM are useful references. Governance teams may pair these with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to map metrics, thresholds, and human oversight into deployment gates.
